questions.q: In an electrical system, which component is like the pump in a water system?
questions.explain: The cell is like the pump. It provides the energy that pushes charge around the circuit, just as a pump pushes water around the pipes.
questions.lo: Name the main components of an electrical system and their functions

notes.0: Wires are like the pipes. They give a path for charge to flow but do not push it. Think about which part supplies the energy.
notes.1: A switch is like a tap. It opens or closes the path but does not push charge. Think about which part supplies the energy.
notes.3: A bulb uses energy, like a water wheel turned by flowing water. Think about which part gives the charge its energy in the first place.

why.right: A cell acts like a pump because it gives charge the energy to move around the circuit.
wrong: A cell acts like a pump because it stores current and releases it into the wires.
A cell acts like a pump because it controls whether the circuit is open or closed.

questions.q: Electric charge in wires is carried by
questions.explain: Electrons are tiny negatively charged particles. In metal wires some electrons are free to move, and they carry the charge around the circuit.
questions.lo: Name the main components of an electrical system and their functions

notes.0: Neutrons have no charge, so they cannot carry electric charge. Think about which particle has a charge and is free to move in a metal.
notes.2: Protons are charged but they are held in the nucleus of each atom and do not move along a wire. Think about which charged particle can move.
notes.3: The atoms in a metal wire stay in place. Electric charge is carried by smaller charged particles that can move between the atoms.

why.right: Electrons carry charge in wires because some of them are free to move between the metal atoms.
wrong: Electrons carry charge in wires because they are the heaviest particles in an atom.
Electrons carry charge in wires because they have no charge and slip easily through metal.

questions.q: Two or more cells connected end to end form a
questions.explain: A battery is two or more cells joined end to end. Joining cells this way gives a larger push to the charge.
questions.lo: Name the main components of an electrical system and their functions

notes.1: A fuse is a safety device with a thin wire that melts when the current is too large. It is not made of cells.
notes.2: A resistor opposes the flow of current. It does not supply energy, so joining cells does not make one.
notes.3: A rheostat is a resistor whose resistance can be changed. It does not supply energy, so joining cells does not make one.

questions.q: In a closed circuit,
questions.explain: A closed circuit is a complete loop with no gaps. Charge can travel all the way round, so current flows.
questions.lo: Identify open and closed circuits

notes.0: An open switch makes a gap in the circuit. A closed circuit has no gaps anywhere in the loop.
notes.1: This describes an open circuit. In a closed circuit the loop is complete, so think about what charge can do in a complete loop.
notes.2: A bulb fails to light when there is a gap in the loop. In a closed circuit the loop is complete.

why.right: Current flows in a closed circuit because there is a complete path for charge to travel round.
wrong: Current flows in a closed circuit because the switch stores charge until it is pressed.
Current flows in a closed circuit because the wires inside it have no resistance at all.

questions.q: A cell, bulb and open switch are connected. The bulb
questions.explain: An open switch leaves a gap in the circuit. No current can flow, so the bulb does not light up.
questions.lo: Identify open and closed circuits

notes.0: A dim bulb still needs some current. An open switch makes a gap, so think about whether any current can flow at all.
notes.2: A bulb only overheats with a current far too large. An open switch makes a gap in the circuit, so think about how much current flows.
notes.3: A bright bulb needs a large current through a complete loop. An open switch makes a gap in the circuit.

why.right: A bulb in a circuit with an open switch stays off because the gap stops current from flowing.
wrong: A bulb in a circuit with an open switch stays off because the switch uses up all the energy.
A bulb in a circuit with an open switch stays off because the cell stops making charge.

questions.q: A wire to a bulb is cut. The circuit is
questions.explain: Cutting a wire makes a gap in the circuit. A circuit with a gap is an open circuit, so no current flows.
questions.lo: Identify open and closed circuits

notes.1: Parallel describes components arranged on separate branches. It does not describe a break in a wire. Think about what a gap does to the loop.
notes.2: A closed circuit is a complete loop. A cut wire leaves a gap, so the loop is no longer complete.

why.right: A circuit with a cut wire is open because the cut leaves a gap in the path for charge.
wrong: A circuit with a cut wire is open because the charge leaks out through the cut ends.
A circuit with a cut wire is open because the cut wire now has no resistance.

questions.q: A bulb lights up when the switch is pressed. The switch is
questions.explain: The bulb lights up, so current is flowing. Current can only flow when the switch is closed and the circuit is complete.
questions.lo: Identify open and closed circuits

notes.0: Removing a switch would leave a gap in the circuit, so the bulb would not light. Think about the switch position that completes the loop.
notes.1: An open switch makes a gap in the circuit, so no current flows. The bulb lit up, so think about which switch position completes the loop.

why.right: A switch that lights a bulb is closed because a closed switch completes the path for charge.
wrong: A switch that lights a bulb is closed because a closed switch gives extra energy to the charge.
A switch that lights a bulb is closed because a closed switch stores charge for the bulb.

questions.q: In a circuit diagram, which component is shown as a long line beside a short line?
questions.explain: The symbol for a cell is a long line beside a short line. The long line is the positive terminal and the short line is the negative terminal.
questions.lo: Identify open and closed circuits

notes.0: A switch is drawn as a break in the wire with a hinged line. Think about which symbol shows two parallel lines of different lengths.
notes.1: A bulb is drawn as a circle with a cross inside. Think about which symbol shows two parallel lines of different lengths.
notes.2: A fixed resistor is drawn as a rectangle. Think about which symbol shows two parallel lines of different lengths.

questions.q: Electric current is the
choices: energy to move a unit charge
rate of flow of electric charge
opposition to the flow of charge
questions.explain: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge. It tells how much charge passes a point in the circuit each second.
questions.lo: Describe current and potential difference and state their SI units

notes.0: Energy to move a unit charge describes potential difference. Current is about the movement of the charge itself, not the energy it carries.
notes.2: Opposition to the flow of charge describes resistance. Current is about the movement of the charge itself.
notes.3: Energy used per unit time describes power. Current is about the movement of the charge itself, not energy.

questions.q: Potential difference is the
choices: opposition to the flow of charge
energy needed to move a unit charge
rate of flow of electric charge
questions.explain: Potential difference is the energy needed to move a unit charge between two points in a circuit. It is measured in volts.
questions.lo: Describe current and potential difference and state their SI units

notes.0: Energy used per unit time describes power. Potential difference is about the energy linked to each unit of charge.
notes.1: Opposition to the flow of charge describes resistance. Potential difference is about the energy linked to each unit of charge.
notes.3: The rate of flow of charge describes current. Potential difference is about the energy linked to each unit of charge.

questions.q: Potential difference is also called
questions.explain: Potential difference is also called voltage because it is measured in volts.
questions.lo: Describe current and potential difference and state their SI units

notes.1: Resistance is a different quantity. It measures how much a component opposes current. Think about the name that comes from the unit of potential difference.
notes.2: Power is a different quantity. It is the energy used per unit time. Think about the name that comes from the unit of potential difference.
notes.3: Current is a different quantity. It is the rate of flow of charge. Think about the name that comes from the unit of potential difference.

questions.q: Resistance is a measure of how much a component
questions.explain: Resistance measures how much a component opposes the flow of current. A larger resistance means a smaller current for the same cell.
questions.lo: Describe resistance and state its SI unit

notes.0: Measuring current is the job of an ammeter. Resistance is a property of a component that affects how easily current passes through it.
notes.1: Pushing charge around a circuit is the job of the cell. Resistance is about how easily current can pass through a component.
notes.2: Storing chemical energy is what a cell does. Resistance is about how easily current can pass through a component.

questions.q: Adding a resistor to a circuit with a bulb makes the bulb
questions.explain: A resistor adds to the total resistance of the circuit. The current becomes smaller, so the bulb is less bright.
questions.lo: Describe resistance and state its SI unit

notes.1: A resistor does not switch current on and off. It changes the size of a steady current. Think about whether the current becomes larger or smaller.
notes.2: A resistor opposes the flow of current, so it changes the current in the bulb. Think about whether the current becomes larger or smaller.
notes.3: A resistor adds resistance to the circuit. More resistance does not give a larger current. Think about what happens to the current through the bulb.

why.right: A bulb dims when a resistor is added because the larger total resistance lowers the current.
wrong: A bulb dims when a resistor is added because the resistor uses up the current before the bulb.
A bulb dims when a resistor is added because the resistor stores some of the charge from the cell.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of current?
questions.explain: Current is measured in amperes (A). The ampere is the SI unit of current.
questions.lo: Match each quantity to its SI unit and measuring instrument

notes.0: The volt is the unit of potential difference, not current. Think about the unit shown on an ammeter.
notes.1: The watt is the unit of power, not current. Think about the unit shown on an ammeter.
notes.3: The ohm is the unit of resistance, not current. Think about the unit shown on an ammeter.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of potential difference?
questions.explain: Potential difference is measured in volts (V). This is why it is also called voltage.
questions.lo: Match each quantity to its SI unit and measuring instrument

notes.0: The watt is the unit of power, not potential difference. Think about the unit shown on a voltmeter.
notes.1: The ohm is the unit of resistance, not potential difference. Think about the unit shown on a voltmeter.
notes.2: The ampere is the unit of current, not potential difference. Think about the unit shown on a voltmeter.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of resistance?
questions.explain: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω). The ohm is the SI unit of resistance.
questions.lo: Match each quantity to its SI unit and measuring instrument

notes.0: The joule is the unit of energy, not resistance. Match each unit to the quantity it measures.
notes.2: The volt is the unit of potential difference, not resistance. Match each unit to the quantity it measures.
notes.3: The ampere is the unit of current, not resistance. Match each unit to the quantity it measures.

questions.q: Which SI unit is not correct?
questions.explain: Current is measured in amperes (A), not volts. The volt is the unit of potential difference. The other three pairs are correct.
questions.lo: Match each quantity to its SI unit and measuring instrument

notes.0: Resistance is measured in ohms, so this pair is correct. The question asks for the pair that is not correct.
notes.1: Energy is measured in joules, so this pair is correct. The question asks for the pair that is not correct.
notes.2: Power is measured in watts, so this pair is correct. The question asks for the pair that is not correct.

questions.q: A reading is 2.5 A. Which quantity is being measured?
questions.explain: The ampere (A) is the unit of current. A reading of 2.5 A is a current reading from an ammeter.
questions.lo: Match each quantity to its SI unit and measuring instrument

notes.1: Potential difference is measured in volts (V). Look at the unit letter A in the reading and match it to its quantity.
notes.2: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω). Look at the unit letter A in the reading and match it to its quantity.
notes.3: Power is measured in watts (W). Look at the unit letter A in the reading and match it to its quantity.

questions.q: A reading is 6 V. Which instrument gave this reading?
questions.explain: The volt (V) is the unit of potential difference. Potential difference is measured with a voltmeter.
questions.lo: Match each quantity to its SI unit and measuring instrument

notes.0: An ammeter measures current in amperes (A). The reading is in volts, so think about which instrument measures potential difference.
notes.1: A fuse is a safety device, not a measuring instrument. The reading is in volts, so think about which instrument measures potential difference.
notes.3: A rheostat changes the resistance in a circuit. It does not give readings. Think about which instrument measures potential difference.

questions.q: A student wants to measure the current through a bulb. Which instrument should she use?
questions.explain: An ammeter measures current. It is connected in series with the bulb so the same current passes through both.
questions.lo: Match each quantity to its SI unit and measuring instrument

notes.0: A rheostat changes the current but does not measure it. Think about which instrument gives a reading in amperes.
notes.2: A voltmeter measures potential difference in volts, not current. Think about which instrument gives a reading in amperes.
notes.3: A thermometer measures temperature, not current. Think about which instrument gives a reading in amperes.

questions.q: In a circuit diagram, a circle with the letter A inside represents
questions.explain: A circle with the letter A inside is the symbol for an ammeter. A stands for amperes, the unit of the current it measures.
questions.lo: Match each quantity to its SI unit and measuring instrument

notes.0: A voltmeter is drawn as a circle with the letter V inside. Think about what the letter A stands for.
notes.1: A cell is drawn as a long line beside a short line. Think about what the letter A stands for.
notes.2: A bulb is drawn as a circle with a cross inside. Think about what the letter A stands for.

questions.q: An ammeter is connected
questions.explain: An ammeter is connected in series with the component. All the current through the component then also passes through the ammeter.
questions.lo: Connect ammeters and voltmeters correctly in a circuit

notes.0: Connecting in parallel is how a voltmeter is used. An ammeter must have the same current flowing through it as the component.
notes.1: An ammeter connected across the cell would let a very large current flow. An ammeter must be on the same path as the component.
notes.3: An ammeter does not supply energy, so it cannot replace the cell. It must have the same current flowing through it as the component.

why.right: An ammeter is placed in series so that the same current flows through it and the component.
wrong: An ammeter is placed in series so that it can add extra current to the component.
An ammeter is placed in series so that it can measure the energy stored in the component.

questions.q: A voltmeter is connected
questions.explain: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component, with one lead on each side of it. It then measures the potential difference across that component.
questions.lo: Connect ammeters and voltmeters correctly in a circuit

notes.1: A voltmeter does not supply energy, so it cannot replace the cell. It must measure between the two ends of the component.
notes.2: Connecting in series is how an ammeter is used. A voltmeter compares the two ends of the component.
notes.3: Replacing the switch would not connect the voltmeter to the two ends of the component. It must measure across the component itself.

why.right: A voltmeter is placed in parallel so that its leads join the two ends of the component.
wrong: A voltmeter is placed in parallel so that all the current passes through the voltmeter first.
A voltmeter is placed in parallel so that it can supply extra voltage to the component.

questions.q: To measure the potential difference across a bulb, the voltmeter is connected
questions.explain: Potential difference is measured across a component. The voltmeter is joined in parallel with the bulb, with one lead on each side of it.
questions.lo: Connect ammeters and voltmeters correctly in a circuit

notes.0: Series connection is used for an ammeter. A voltmeter must be connected to the two ends of the bulb to measure across it.
notes.2: A voltmeter in series with the cell is not connected across the bulb. It must be joined to the two ends of the bulb.
notes.3: Replacing the bulb removes the very component being measured. The voltmeter must be joined to the two ends of the bulb.

why.right: A voltmeter goes in parallel with a bulb because potential difference is measured across its two ends.
wrong: A voltmeter goes in parallel with a bulb because the voltmeter must carry all of the bulb's current.
A voltmeter goes in parallel with a bulb because the voltmeter pushes extra charge through the bulb.

questions.q: To measure the current through a resistor, the ammeter is connected
questions.explain: Current is measured through a component. The ammeter is joined in series with the resistor, so the same current passes through both.
questions.lo: Connect ammeters and voltmeters correctly in a circuit

notes.0: Replacing the resistor removes the component being measured and changes the current. The ammeter must have the resistor's current flowing through it.
notes.2: Parallel connection is used for a voltmeter. An ammeter must have the same current flowing through it as the resistor.
notes.3: An ammeter across the cell would let a very large current flow and does not measure the resistor. It must carry the resistor's current.

why.right: An ammeter goes in series with a resistor because the same current then flows through both of them.
wrong: An ammeter goes in series with a resistor because the ammeter measures the energy the resistor stores.
An ammeter goes in series with a resistor because the ammeter adds more current to the resistor.

questions.q: Electrical insulators have
questions.explain: Electrical insulators have very high resistance. Almost no current can flow through them, so they are used to cover wires and plugs.
questions.lo: Classify materials by their resistance

notes.1: Adjustable resistance describes a rheostat. Insulators are materials that let almost no current pass through.
notes.2: Low resistance describes good conductors such as copper. Insulators are materials that let almost no current pass through.
notes.3: No resistance would let current flow very easily, which is the opposite of an insulator. Insulators let almost no current pass through.

questions.q: Copper is used for connecting wires because its resistance is
questions.explain: Copper has low resistance, so current flows through it easily and little energy is wasted as heat in the connecting wires.
questions.lo: Classify materials by their resistance

notes.0: Adjustable resistance describes a rheostat. Connecting wires need to let current pass easily all the time.
notes.1: High resistance would make the wires heat up and reduce the current. Connecting wires need to let current pass easily.
notes.3: Very high resistance describes insulators such as plastic. Connecting wires need to let current pass easily.

why.right: Copper suits connecting wires because current passes through it easily and little energy is lost as heat.
wrong: Copper suits connecting wires because it stops too much current from reaching the components.
Copper suits connecting wires because it heats up quickly and gives a warning of a fault.

questions.q: Plastic covers wires because it is
choices: an insulator with very high resistance
questions.explain: Plastic is an insulator with very high resistance. It stops current from passing from the wire to anyone who touches it.
questions.lo: Classify materials by their resistance

notes.0: A conductor with low resistance would let current pass to anyone touching the wire. A wire covering must stop current from passing.
notes.1: A variable resistor is a component used inside circuits. A wire covering must stop current from passing through it.
notes.2: A conductor, even one with high resistance, still lets some current pass. A wire covering must stop current from passing through it.

why.right: Plastic is used to cover wires because almost no current can pass through it to a person.
wrong: Plastic is used to cover wires because it carries extra current safely along the wire.
Plastic is used to cover wires because it stores the charge that leaks from the wire.

questions.q: Which material is a conductor that converts much electrical energy to heat?
questions.explain: Nichrome is a conductor with high resistance. When current passes through it, much electrical energy is converted to heat, so it is used in heating elements.
questions.lo: Classify materials by their resistance

notes.0: Copper is a conductor with low resistance, so little energy becomes heat in it. Think about a conductor with high resistance.
notes.1: Glass is an insulator, so almost no current passes through it. The material asked for must be a conductor.
notes.3: Silver is a conductor with very low resistance, so little energy becomes heat in it. Think about a conductor with high resistance.

why.right: Nichrome heats up strongly because its high resistance converts much electrical energy to heat.
wrong: Nichrome heats up strongly because it is an insulator that traps heat inside the wire.
Nichrome heats up strongly because it stores electrical energy and releases it later as heat.

questions.q: Which material is a conductor with low resistance?
questions.explain: Silver is a metal and a very good conductor with low resistance. Current passes through it easily.
questions.lo: Classify materials by their resistance

notes.1: Tungsten is a conductor, but its resistance is high, which is why it glows in a filament bulb. Think about a metal that lets current pass very easily.
notes.2: Glass is an insulator with very high resistance. The material asked for must be a conductor that lets current pass easily.
notes.3: Plastic is an insulator with very high resistance. The material asked for must be a conductor that lets current pass easily.

questions.q: Resistors with only one path for current are arranged in
questions.explain: In a series circuit the components are connected one after another, so there is only one path for the current.
questions.lo: Predict how adding resistors in series or parallel changes the current

notes.0: In a parallel arrangement the current splits into separate branches, so there is more than one path. Think about components joined one after another.
notes.2: A short circuit is a fault where current takes a path with almost no resistance. It is not a way of arranging resistors.

questions.q: A second resistor is added in series. The ammeter reading will
questions.explain: A second resistor in series adds to the total resistance. With more resistance and the same cell, the current becomes smaller, so the ammeter reading decreases.
questions.lo: Predict how adding resistors in series or parallel changes the current

notes.1: The resistor adds resistance to the only path, so the current does change. Think about whether more resistance gives more or less current.
notes.2: Adding a resistor in series makes the total resistance larger, not smaller. Think about what a larger resistance does to the current.

why.right: Adding a resistor in series lowers the current because the total resistance of the single path increases.
wrong: Adding a resistor in series lowers the current because each resistor uses up part of the current.
Adding a resistor in series lowers the current because the resistor stores some of the charge from the cell.

questions.q: A second resistor is added in parallel. The ammeter reading will
questions.explain: A second resistor in parallel gives the current an extra path. The total resistance decreases, so the total current increases and the ammeter reading increases.
questions.lo: Predict how adding resistors in series or parallel changes the current

notes.0: A resistor added in parallel gives the current an extra path. Think about whether an extra path makes the total resistance larger or smaller.
notes.1: An extra parallel path changes the total resistance of the circuit. Think about whether more paths let more or less charge flow.

why.right: Adding a resistor in parallel raises the current because the extra path lowers the total resistance.
wrong: Adding a resistor in parallel raises the current because each resistor adds its own current to the circuit.
Adding a resistor in parallel raises the current because the extra resistor gives the charge more energy.

questions.q: A second resistor is added in series. The overall resistance will
questions.explain: Resistors in series add together. A second resistor in series makes the overall resistance larger.
questions.lo: Predict how adding resistors in series or parallel changes the current

notes.0: Each resistor in series opposes the current, and their effects add together. Think about what adding another one does to the total.
notes.2: A decrease happens when a resistor is added in parallel. In series, the current must pass through every resistor in turn.

why.right: Resistors in series raise the overall resistance because the current must pass through each one in turn.
wrong: Resistors in series raise the overall resistance because they use up more of the current.
Resistors in series raise the overall resistance because they give the current an extra path.

questions.q: A second resistor is added in parallel. The bulb will become
questions.explain: A resistor added in parallel with the existing resistor gives an extra path. The total resistance decreases, the current increases and the bulb becomes brighter.
questions.lo: Predict how adding resistors in series or parallel changes the current

notes.1: An extra parallel path changes the total resistance and so changes the current through the bulb. Think about whether the current rises or falls.
notes.2: A bulb becomes dimmer when a resistor is added in series. A parallel resistor gives an extra path, which changes the total resistance.

why.right: A parallel resistor brightens the bulb because the total resistance falls and a larger current flows.
wrong: A parallel resistor brightens the bulb because the resistor adds its own current to the bulb.
A parallel resistor brightens the bulb because the total resistance rises and pushes more charge.

questions.q: After a second resistor is added, the bulb becomes brighter. It was added in
questions.explain: Adding a resistor in parallel lowers the total resistance, so the current increases and the bulb becomes brighter. A resistor in series would make it dimmer.
questions.lo: Predict how adding resistors in series or parallel changes the current

notes.0: If the resistor replaced the bulb, there would be no bulb left to light up. Think about which arrangement lowers the total resistance.
notes.1: A resistor in series raises the total resistance, which makes the bulb dimmer. Think about which arrangement lowers the total resistance.

why.right: A parallel resistor makes the bulb brighter because the extra path lowers the total resistance.
wrong: A parallel resistor makes the bulb brighter because it adds its own energy to the bulb.
A parallel resistor makes the bulb brighter because it raises the total resistance of the circuit.

questions.q: A rheostat changes the current by changing its
questions.explain: A rheostat is a variable resistor. Moving its slider changes its resistance, and this changes the current in the circuit.
questions.lo: Predict how a variable resistor changes current and brightness

notes.0: A rheostat does not supply energy, so it does not change the cell's voltage. Think about what moving the slider changes inside the rheostat.
notes.1: A power rating is a label on an appliance and is not changed by a slider. Think about what moving the slider changes inside the rheostat.
notes.2: A rheostat does not add or remove cells. Think about what moving the slider changes inside the rheostat.

why.right: A rheostat changes the current because moving its slider changes the length of wire the current passes through.
wrong: A rheostat changes the current because moving its slider changes how much charge the rheostat stores.
A rheostat changes the current because moving its slider changes the voltage that the cell supplies.

questions.q: The resistance of a rheostat is increased. The bulb will become
questions.explain: Increasing the resistance of the rheostat makes the total resistance larger. The current becomes smaller, so the bulb becomes less bright.
questions.lo: Predict how a variable resistor changes current and brightness

notes.0: Changing the rheostat's resistance changes the current in the whole circuit. Think about whether more resistance gives a larger or smaller current.
notes.2: More resistance does not give a larger current. Think about what a larger resistance does to the current through the bulb.

why.right: A bulb dims when rheostat resistance rises because a larger resistance gives a smaller current.
wrong: A bulb dims when rheostat resistance rises because the rheostat uses up the current first.
A bulb dims when rheostat resistance rises because the rheostat stores charge meant for the bulb.

questions.q: The resistance of a rheostat is decreased. The ammeter reading will
questions.explain: Decreasing the resistance of the rheostat makes the total resistance smaller. A larger current flows, so the ammeter reading increases.
questions.lo: Predict how a variable resistor changes current and brightness

notes.1: Changing the rheostat's resistance changes the current in the whole circuit. Think about whether less resistance gives a larger or smaller current.
notes.2: Less resistance means less opposition to the current. Think about what this does to the amount of current that flows.

why.right: The ammeter reading rises when rheostat resistance falls because less opposition lets more current flow.
wrong: The ammeter reading rises when rheostat resistance falls because the rheostat now adds current.
The ammeter reading rises when rheostat resistance falls because the cell now makes more charge.

questions.q: A dimmer is turned so the lights become dimmer. The resistance has
questions.explain: The lights became dimmer, so the current became smaller. A smaller current means the resistance of the dimmer has increased.
questions.lo: Predict how a variable resistor changes current and brightness

notes.0: Less resistance would give a larger current and brighter lights. The lights became dimmer, so think about how the resistance changed.
notes.1: If the resistance did not change, the current and brightness would not change. Turning the dimmer changed the brightness.

why.right: Lights become dimmer when resistance increases because a larger resistance gives a smaller current.
wrong: Lights become dimmer when resistance increases because the dimmer uses up part of the current.
Lights become dimmer when resistance increases because the dimmer lowers the mains supply voltage.

questions.q: The ammeter reading rises when a rheostat slider is moved. The resistance has
questions.explain: A rising ammeter reading means a larger current. A larger current flows when the resistance of the rheostat decreases.
questions.lo: Predict how a variable resistor changes current and brightness

notes.0: More resistance would give a smaller current and a lower reading. The reading rose, so think about how the resistance changed.
notes.2: If the resistance did not change, the current would not change. The reading rose, so the resistance must have changed.

why.right: A rising ammeter reading shows lower resistance because less opposition lets more current flow.
wrong: A rising ammeter reading shows lower resistance because the rheostat now adds charge to the circuit.
A rising ammeter reading shows lower resistance because the cell now supplies a higher voltage.

questions.q: A heating element is usually made of
questions.explain: Nichrome is a conductor with high resistance and a high melting point. It converts much electrical energy to heat without melting.
questions.lo: Identify the chemical, heating or magnetic effect in an application

notes.0: Glass is an insulator, so current cannot pass through it to produce heat. A heating element must be a conductor.
notes.1: Copper has low resistance, so little electrical energy becomes heat in it. A heating element needs a conductor with high resistance.
notes.2: Plastic is an insulator and would melt when hot. A heating element must be a conductor that can get very hot.

why.right: Heating elements use nichrome because its high resistance turns much electrical energy into heat.
wrong: Heating elements use nichrome because its low resistance lets it store more heat.
Heating elements use nichrome because it is an insulator that keeps the heat in.

questions.q: Surgical tweezers are coated with a thin layer of silver. Which effect is used?
questions.explain: Coating tweezers with silver is electroplating. Current passes through a solution and deposits a thin layer of metal, which is the chemical effect of current.
questions.lo: Identify the chemical, heating or magnetic effect in an application

notes.1: The heating effect makes things hot, as in a kettle. Coating an object with a metal layer uses a different effect of current.
notes.2: The magnetic effect produces a magnetic field, as in an electromagnet. Coating an object with a metal layer uses a different effect of current.

why.right: Electroplating uses the chemical effect because current through a solution deposits metal on an object.
wrong: Electroplating uses the chemical effect because current melts the metal so it drips on the object.
Electroplating uses the chemical effect because current magnetises metal so it sticks to the object.

questions.q: A rice cooker cooks rice. Which effect of current is used?
questions.explain: A rice cooker has a heating element. Current through the element produces heat, which cooks the rice. This is the heating effect of current.
questions.lo: Identify the chemical, heating or magnetic effect in an application

notes.0: The magnetic effect produces a magnetic field, as in an electromagnet. Cooking rice needs the food to get hot.
notes.2: The chemical effect is used in electroplating. Cooking rice needs the food to get hot.

why.right: A rice cooker uses the heating effect because current in its element converts electrical energy to heat.
wrong: A rice cooker uses the heating effect because current reacts with the water to release heat.
A rice cooker uses the heating effect because current passes into the rice grains and cooks them.

questions.q: An MRI machine produces images of soft tissues. Which effect is used?
questions.explain: An MRI machine uses a very strong electromagnet. Current in its coils produces a strong magnetic field, which is the magnetic effect of current.
questions.lo: Identify the chemical, heating or magnetic effect in an application

notes.0: The chemical effect is used in electroplating. Think about what large coils carrying current in a scanner produce.
notes.1: The heating effect is used in kettles and rice cookers. An MRI scanner does not make images by heating the body.

why.right: An MRI machine uses the magnetic effect because current in its coils produces a strong magnetic field.
wrong: An MRI machine uses the magnetic effect because current coats the body in a thin metal layer.
An MRI machine uses the magnetic effect because current heats the tissues until they glow.

questions.q: A knee implant is electroplated with titanium. Which effect is used?
questions.explain: Electroplating uses the chemical effect of current. Current through a solution deposits a thin layer of titanium on the implant.
questions.lo: Identify the chemical, heating or magnetic effect in an application

notes.0: The magnetic effect produces a magnetic field, as in an electromagnet. Electroplating deposits a metal layer, which uses a different effect.
notes.1: The heating effect makes things hot, as in a kettle. Electroplating deposits a metal layer, which uses a different effect.

why.right: Electroplating an implant uses the chemical effect because current through a solution deposits metal on it.
wrong: Electroplating an implant uses the chemical effect because current heats the metal until it melts onto it.
Electroplating an implant uses the chemical effect because current magnetises the metal so it sticks to it.

questions.q: The strength of an electromagnet increases when
choices: a plastic core is placed in the coil
an iron core is placed in the coil
questions.explain: An iron core inside the coil becomes magnetised by the current. Its magnetism adds to the coil's field, so the electromagnet becomes stronger.
questions.lo: Identify the chemical, heating or magnetic effect in an application

notes.0: Without the coil there is no current to produce a magnetic field. The coil is what makes an electromagnet work.
notes.1: Plastic is not a magnetic material, so it does not strengthen the field. Think about a core material that can be magnetised.
notes.2: Switching off the current stops the electromagnet from working at all. Its magnetism comes from the current in the coil.

why.right: An iron core strengthens an electromagnet because the iron becomes magnetised and adds to the field.
wrong: An iron core strengthens an electromagnet because the iron adds extra current to the coil.
An iron core strengthens an electromagnet because the iron stores charge from the coil.

questions.q: A compass needle near a wire deflects. This shows the
questions.explain: A current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it. This field pushes on the compass needle, so the needle deflects. This is the magnetic effect of current.
questions.lo: Identify the chemical, heating or magnetic effect in an application

notes.1: Heat from a wire does not turn a compass needle. Think about what normally makes a compass needle point in a direction.
notes.2: The chemical effect deposits metal from a solution, as in electroplating. Think about what normally makes a compass needle point in a direction.

why.right: A compass needle deflects near a current because the current produces a magnetic field around the wire.
wrong: A compass needle deflects near a current because heat from the wire pushes on the needle.
A compass needle deflects near a current because charge flows out of the wire into the needle.

questions.q: Plugging many appliances into one socket can cause
questions.explain: Plugging many appliances into one socket overloads it. The large total current heats the wires strongly, which can cause an electrical fire.
questions.lo: State how changes to an electrical system cause hazards

notes.0: More appliances draw more current, and more current makes the wires hotter, not cooler. Think about what too much heat can lead to.
notes.1: Plugging in appliances does not make a magnet. Think about what a very large current does to the temperature of the wires.
notes.2: Each appliance draws its own current, so the total current through the socket gets larger. Think about what this does to the wires.

why.right: Overloading a socket is dangerous because the large total current makes the wires overheat.
wrong: Overloading a socket is dangerous because each appliance takes current away from the others.
Overloading a socket is dangerous because the socket stores the extra charge until it bursts.

questions.q: The insulation on a wire is worn out. What is the hazard?
questions.explain: Worn insulation leaves the metal wire exposed. Anyone who touches the exposed live wire can get an electric shock.
questions.lo: State how changes to an electrical system cause hazards

notes.0: Worn insulation does not break the metal wire, so current can still flow. Think about what can happen if someone touches the bare metal.
notes.1: Damage to a wire's covering does not change the fuse. Think about what can happen if someone touches the bare metal.
notes.2: The metal inside is still a conductor. It is the plastic covering that has worn away, leaving the metal bare.

why.right: Worn insulation is a hazard because current can pass from the bare wire through a person.
wrong: Worn insulation is a hazard because the bare wire stops conducting and the appliance fails.
Worn insulation is a hazard because the bare wire draws charge out of the fuse.

questions.q: Why should a hairdryer not be used with wet hands?
questions.explain: Water, especially tap water with dissolved substances, conducts electricity. Wet hands let current pass into the body more easily, so there is a risk of electric shock.
questions.lo: State how changes to an electrical system cause hazards

notes.0: Water does not melt a fuse. Think about what water does when it touches something carrying current.
notes.2: Tap water is not an insulator. If it were, wet hands would be safer, not more dangerous.
notes.3: Wet skin has lower resistance than dry skin, not higher. Think about how easily current can pass through water.

why.right: Wet hands are dangerous near appliances because water lets current pass into the body easily.
wrong: Wet hands are dangerous near appliances because water blocks current and makes the appliance overheat.
Wet hands are dangerous near appliances because water stores charge and releases it later.

questions.q: A damaged circuit draws a very large current. What is the hazard?
choices: wires overheat and may cause a fire
questions.explain: A very large current produces a lot of heat in the wires. The wires can overheat, melt their insulation and start a fire.
questions.lo: State how changes to an electrical system cause hazards

notes.0: A large current does not change a metal into an insulator. Think about what a large current does to the temperature of the wires.
notes.1: A large current would not make a bulb dimmer. Think about what a large current does to the temperature of the wires.
notes.2: A very large current is the opposite of zero current. Think about what so much current does to the temperature of the wires.

why.right: A very large current is a hazard because its heating effect makes the wires overheat.
wrong: A very large current is a hazard because the wires run out of charge and stop working.
A very large current is a hazard because the current flows out of the wires into the air.

questions.q: A fuse protects an appliance by
choices: melting when the current is too large
questions.explain: A fuse contains a thin wire with a low melting point. When the current is too large, the wire melts and breaks the circuit, which stops the current.
questions.lo: State precautions and safety devices for using electricity at home

notes.0: A fuse does not store charge. It is a thin wire that reacts to how large the current is.
notes.1: A fuse never increases the current. It is there to stop a current that has become too large.
notes.2: A fuse does not change the voltage. It is a thin wire that reacts to how large the current is.

why.right: A fuse protects an appliance because a large current heats its thin wire until it breaks the circuit.
wrong: A fuse protects an appliance because its thin wire stores the extra current until it is safe.
A fuse protects an appliance because its thin wire turns the extra current into light.

questions.q: Which device trips and cuts off current when a fault occurs?
questions.explain: A circuit breaker trips when a fault causes too large a current. This cuts off the current, and it can be reset after the fault is fixed.
questions.lo: State precautions and safety devices for using electricity at home

notes.1: A voltmeter only measures potential difference. It cannot cut off the current. Think about a safety device that can be reset.
notes.2: A rheostat changes resistance to adjust the current but does not trip on a fault. Think about a safety device that can be reset.
notes.3: An ammeter only measures current. It cannot cut off the current. Think about a safety device that can be reset.

questions.q: A fuse has melted. After the fault is corrected, you should
questions.explain: A melted fuse has a broken wire, so the circuit stays open. Once the fault is fixed, a new fuse of the correct rating is fitted.
questions.lo: State precautions and safety devices for using electricity at home

notes.0: A melted fuse has a broken wire, so it cannot complete the circuit again. Think about what restores the protection.
notes.2: A copper wire would not melt when the current is too large, so there would be no protection. This is dangerous.
notes.3: Without a fuse the circuit is either broken or unprotected. The appliance needs working protection after the fault is fixed.

why.right: A melted fuse must be replaced because its broken wire leaves a gap in the circuit.
wrong: A melted fuse must be replaced because its wire has used up all of its stored charge.
A melted fuse must be replaced because its wire now lets too much current pass through.

questions.q: What should be done before washing an electrical appliance?
choices: use a wet cloth on the plug
questions.explain: Switching off the power supply stops current from reaching the appliance. Water conducts electricity, so washing a live appliance could give an electric shock.
questions.lo: State precautions and safety devices for using electricity at home

notes.0: Water conducts electricity, so a wet cloth on a plug can lead to an electric shock. Think about how to make sure no current reaches the appliance.
notes.1: Insulation protects people from the metal wires. Removing it exposes the wires and makes a shock more likely.
notes.3: A switched-on appliance can carry current. With water, this can cause an electric shock. Think about stopping the current first.

why.right: Switching off before washing is safe because no current can then pass through the water to a person.
wrong: Switching off before washing is safe because water becomes an insulator when the power is off.
Switching off before washing is safe because the appliance then keeps its charge locked inside.

questions.q: A two-pin plug does not fit a three-pin socket. You should use
choices: your fingers to open the hole
a metal object in the hole
a wire pushed into the hole
questions.explain: A plug adaptor is designed to connect a two-pin plug safely to a three-pin socket. Fingers, metal objects or wires in a socket can cause an electric shock.
questions.lo: State precautions and safety devices for using electricity at home

notes.1: Putting fingers into a socket can give an electric shock. A safe way is one that keeps the body away from the socket's live parts.
notes.2: Metal conducts electricity, so a metal object in a socket can give an electric shock. A safe way keeps the body away from live parts.
notes.3: A bare wire conducts electricity, so pushing one into a socket can give an electric shock. A safe way keeps the body away from live parts.

why.right: A plug adaptor is the safe choice because it is designed to connect the plug without exposing live parts.
wrong: A plug adaptor is the safe choice because it changes the mains voltage to suit a two-pin plug.
A plug adaptor is the safe choice because it stores extra current for the appliance to use.

questions.q: Power is the
choices: electrical energy used per unit time
energy to move a unit charge
questions.explain: Power is the electrical energy used per unit time. It tells how quickly an appliance uses electrical energy.
questions.lo: Explain what power is and state its SI unit

notes.0: The rate of flow of charge describes current. Power links energy with time, not charge.
notes.1: Opposition to current describes resistance. Power links energy with time.
notes.3: Energy to move a unit charge describes potential difference. Power links energy with time, not charge.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of power?
questions.explain: The SI unit of power is the watt (W). One watt is one joule of energy used each second.
questions.lo: Explain what power is and state its SI unit

notes.0: The volt is the unit of potential difference, not power. Think about the unit that equals one joule per second.
notes.2: The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power, and it is not an SI unit. Think about the unit that equals one joule per second.
notes.3: The joule is the unit of energy, not power. Power is energy used per second, so it has its own unit.

questions.q: An oven is rated 2 kW. What is its power in watts?
questions.lo: Explain what power is and state its SI unit

notes.0: This uses 1 kW as 10 W. Kilo means one thousand, so check how many watts make one kilowatt.
notes.1: This uses 1 kW as 10 000 W. Kilo means one thousand, so check how many watts make one kilowatt.
notes.2: This uses 1 kW as 100 W. Kilo means one thousand, so check how many watts make one kilowatt.

why.right: Kilowatts are changed to watts by multiplying by 1000, since kilo means one thousand.
wrong: Kilowatts are changed to watts by multiplying by 100, since kilo means one hundred.
Kilowatts are changed to watts by multiplying by 10 000, since kilo means ten thousand.

questions.q: Electrical energy (kWh) =
questions.explain: Power is the energy used per unit time. So energy used = power × time. With power in kW and time in h, the energy is in kWh.
questions.lo: Calculate electrical energy in kWh and its cost

notes.0: Dividing time by power does not give energy. Power is the energy used in each hour, so think about how to get the total for many hours.
notes.2: Dividing power by time gives a smaller answer for longer use, but using an appliance for longer uses more energy. Think about how the total grows.
notes.3: Power and time are different quantities, so they cannot be added. Think about how the total energy grows with each extra hour.

why.right: Electrical energy is power multiplied by time because power is the energy used in each hour.
wrong: Electrical energy is power multiplied by time because power and time are both forms of energy.
Electrical energy is power multiplied by time because power grows the longer an appliance runs.

questions.q: 1 kWh is the energy used by a
questions.explain: 1 kWh is the energy used by a 1 kW (1000 W) appliance switched on for one hour.
questions.lo: Calculate electrical energy in kWh and its cost

notes.0: The kilowatt-hour uses hours, not seconds. Look at the time in the name of the unit.
notes.1: 100 W is only 0.1 kW. Check how many watts make one kilowatt.
notes.2: 1 W is only 0.001 kW. Check how many watts make one kilowatt.

questions.q: A 2 kW heater is used for 3 h. How much energy is used?
questions.explain: Energy = power × time = 2 kW × 3 h = 6 kWh.
questions.lo: Calculate electrical energy in kWh and its cost

notes.0: This divides the power by the time. Using the heater for longer uses more energy, so think about which operation makes the total grow.
notes.1: This adds the power and the time. Power and time are different quantities, so they cannot be added.
notes.3: This divides the time by the power. Energy grows with both power and time, so think about which operation links them.

why.right: Energy in kWh is found by multiplying the power in kW by the time in hours.
wrong: Energy in kWh is found by dividing the power in kW by the time in hours.
Energy in kWh is found by adding the power in kW to the time in hours.

questions.q: A 500 W iron is used for 2 h. How much energy is used?
questions.explain: 500 W = 0.5 kW. Energy = power × time = 0.5 kW × 2 h = 1 kWh.
questions.lo: Calculate electrical energy in kWh and its cost

notes.1: This divides 500 by 2 and does not change watts to kilowatts. Change 500 W to kW first, then use energy = power × time.
notes.2: This multiplies 500 W by 2 h without changing watts to kilowatts. An answer in kWh needs the power in kW.
notes.3: This changes 500 W to kW correctly but then divides by the time. Using the iron for longer uses more energy.

why.right: Energy in kWh is found by changing 500 W to 0.5 kW, then multiplying by the time in hours.
wrong: Energy in kWh is found by multiplying 500 W by the time in hours, with no change of unit.
Energy in kWh is found by changing 500 W to 0.5 kW, then dividing by the time in hours.

questions.q: Energy used is 4 kWh at 30 cents per kWh. What is the cost?
questions.explain: Cost = energy × cost per kWh = 4 kWh × 30 cents = 120 cents = $1.20.
questions.lo: Calculate electrical energy in kWh and its cost

notes.0: This changes 120 cents to dollars wrongly. There are 100 cents in a dollar, so check the conversion.
notes.1: This changes 120 cents to dollars wrongly. There are 100 cents in a dollar, so check the conversion.
notes.2: This divides 30 by 4 instead of multiplying. Using more energy costs more, so the cost grows with each kWh.

why.right: Electricity cost is found by multiplying the energy in kWh by the cost of each kWh.
wrong: Electricity cost is found by dividing the energy in kWh by the cost of each kWh.
Electricity cost is found by adding the energy in kWh to the cost of each kWh.

questions.q: A 1.5 kW heater runs for 2 h. The tariff is 20 cents per kWh. Cost?
questions.explain: Energy = 1.5 kW × 2 h = 3 kWh. Cost = 3 kWh × 20 cents = 60 cents = $0.60.
questions.lo: Calculate electrical energy in kWh and its cost

notes.0: This changes 60 cents to dollars wrongly. There are 100 cents in a dollar, so check the conversion.
notes.1: This multiplies the power by the tariff but leaves out the time. Work out the energy in kWh first.
notes.3: This treats 60 cents as 60 dollars. There are 100 cents in a dollar, so check the conversion.

why.right: The cost of running an appliance is found by multiplying the power, the time and the tariff together.
wrong: The cost of running an appliance is found by multiplying the power by the tariff, leaving out the time.
The cost of running an appliance is found by dividing the power by the time, then multiplying by the tariff.

questions.q: A 2 kW kettle used 4 kWh of energy. For how long was it used?
questions.explain: Energy = power × time, so time = energy ÷ power = 4 kWh ÷ 2 kW = 2 h.
questions.lo: Calculate electrical energy in kWh and its cost

notes.1: This divides the power by the energy. Rearrange energy = power × time to make time the subject.
notes.2: This multiplies the energy by the power. Rearrange energy = power × time to make time the subject.
notes.3: This adds the energy and the power. They are different quantities, so rearrange energy = power × time instead.

why.right: Time of use is found by dividing the energy used in kWh by the power in kW.
wrong: Time of use is found by multiplying the energy used in kWh by the power in kW.
Time of use is found by dividing the power in kW by the energy used in kWh.

questions.q: An appliance used 6 kWh in 3 h. What is its power?
questions.explain: Energy = power × time, so power = energy ÷ time = 6 kWh ÷ 3 h = 2 kW.
questions.lo: Calculate electrical energy in kWh and its cost

notes.0: This adds the energy and the time. They are different quantities, so rearrange energy = power × time instead.
notes.2: This divides the time by the energy. Rearrange energy = power × time to make power the subject.
notes.3: This multiplies the energy by the time. Rearrange energy = power × time to make power the subject.

why.right: Power is found by dividing the energy used in kWh by the time in hours.
wrong: Power is found by multiplying the energy used in kWh by the time in hours.
Power is found by dividing the time in hours by the energy used in kWh.

questions.q: Standby power is used when appliances are
choices: left on at the power socket
questions.explain: Appliances left on at the power socket still use a small amount of power to stay ready, for example to respond to a remote control. This is standby power.
questions.lo: Suggest ways to reduce household electrical energy consumption

notes.0: Being fully charged is about a battery, not standby. Think about appliances that are not in use but are still connected and switched on.
notes.2: An unplugged appliance has no connection to the supply, so it uses no power at all. Think about appliances that are still connected.
notes.3: Switching off at the socket stops all current to the appliance, so it uses no power. Standby needs the supply to stay on.

why.right: Standby power is used because an appliance left on at the socket still draws a small current to stay ready.
wrong: Standby power is used because an appliance switched off at the socket stores energy to use later.
Standby power is used because the socket keeps pushing current into an unplugged appliance.

questions.q: Which habit reduces electrical energy consumption?
choices: using the air conditioner all day
using an electric hot water dispenser
switching off the water heater after use
questions.explain: Switching off the water heater after use stops it from using electrical energy when hot water is not needed. The other habits keep appliances using energy.
questions.lo: Suggest ways to reduce household electrical energy consumption

notes.0: A TV on standby still uses some electrical energy. Think about a habit that stops an appliance using energy when it is not needed.
notes.1: An air conditioner has a high power rating, so using it all day uses a lot of energy. Think about a habit that stops energy use when not needed.
notes.2: An electric hot water dispenser keeps heating water all the time, which uses energy. Think about a habit that stops energy use when not needed.

why.right: Turning off an appliance after use saves energy because it uses no electrical energy while it is off.
wrong: Turning off an appliance after use saves energy because it stores extra energy for the next use.
Turning off an appliance after use saves energy because it lowers the appliance's power rating.

questions.q: Which appliance energy label should you choose to save energy?
questions.explain: On an energy label, more ticks means the appliance is more energy efficient. It uses less electrical energy to do the same job.
questions.lo: Suggest ways to reduce household electrical energy consumption

notes.0: A higher power rating means the appliance uses energy faster, so it costs more to run. Think about what the ticks on the label show.
notes.1: Fewer ticks means the appliance is less energy efficient. Think about which end of the tick scale saves energy.
notes.3: Without a label there is no information about energy efficiency. The label is what helps compare appliances.

why.right: More ticks on an energy label save energy because they show the appliance is more energy efficient.
wrong: More ticks on an energy label save energy because they show the appliance has a higher power rating.
More ticks on an energy label save energy because they show the appliance draws a larger current.

questions.q: Switching from an air conditioner to a fan saves energy because the fan
questions.explain: A fan has a much lower power rating than an air conditioner. It uses less electrical energy each hour, so switching to a fan saves energy.
questions.lo: Suggest ways to reduce household electrical energy consumption

notes.1: A higher power rating would mean using more energy each hour, not less. Think about how the two power ratings compare.
notes.2: A larger current would mean using more energy, not less. Think about how the power ratings of the two appliances compare.
notes.3: A fan does use electricity to turn its motor. It just uses less of it. Think about how the two power ratings compare.

why.right: A fan saves energy compared to an air conditioner because it uses less electrical energy each hour.
wrong: A fan saves energy compared to an air conditioner because it runs without any electrical energy.
A fan saves energy compared to an air conditioner because it draws a larger current from the supply.
